case_study_insert.main_stem: Quarryfield Recycled Aggregates (QRAG) is a partnership in the sustainable construction materials sector, employing a workforce of 42. Founded in 2006 by Daniel Okoro and Faith Okoro, the business supplies recycled aggregate to civil engineers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. QRAG plans to invest $800,000 in a mobile crushing and screening plant, financed by a $520,000 bank loan and $280,000 from the sale of surplus land. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. QRAG faces two problems: a contamination defect rate of 3.9% and high absenteeism.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: The crushing plant processed 28,000 tonnes of recycled aggregate last quarter at a contamination defect rate of 3.9%, down from 5.7% a year ago. Customer complaints about grading fell from 41 to 18 per month. Average delivery time is 3.8 days. Site waste is 4.6% of input. A survey of 450 civil engineers found that 61% would specify more recycled aggregate if it met a certified standard, and 54% check environmental credentials on tender documents. A training review shows 16 of 42 site staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new screening plant; off-the-job courses at the training centre cost $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Quarryfield Recycled Aggregates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing debt-service costs for borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.05 to $13.77 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across construction. (3) Wholesale fuel and machinery input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while construction inflation is 6.2% and infrastructure spending grew 3.6%.

questions.question_text: QRAG is funding its $800,000 crushing plant partly with $280,000 from the sale of surplus land. Explain two advantages of using this sale of assets rather than a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $280,000 from selling surplus land is a one-off internal source that requires no interest or repayment, unlike additional borrowing, so QRAG can service the remaining $520,000 bank loan from the $6.00 contribution per unit without raising its fixed costs of $420,000 a year while absenteeism disrupts output.

Point 2: Selling land that is not needed for operations releases cash while keeping decision-making with the two partners, Daniel and Faith Okoro, and fits the flat, laissez-faire structure. A larger loan would require more collateral and covenants over the new screening plant; using the asset sale avoids that risk and helps QRAG respond to the 9.4% rise in fuel and machinery costs without extra debt.

Keeping the partnership's equity intact also means Daniel and Faith Okoro retain full control of the $800,000 investment, and the released cash can fund the $700 training needed for the 16 untrained staff rather than paying extra interest to a lender.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of asset sale over extra borrowing (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to QRAG's partnership and expansion.

questions.question_text: QRAG wants to win more recycled-aggregate contracts. Consider direct tendering to civil engineers, launching an online ordering platform, or sponsoring a construction industry event. Which should QRAG choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Direct tendering to civil engineers: Prepared bids can highlight the 61% of 450 surveyed engineers who would specify recycled aggregate if certified and the 54% who check environmental credentials, building close relationships for a partnership of 42. Tendering is slow, staff-intensive and costly per unsuccessful bid, and with a 3.9% contamination rate QRAG must prove quality before bids are credible.

Online ordering platform: A simple portal can publish certification and environmental data, take repeat orders and streamline the 3.8-day delivery time, reaching engineers beyond the local area at low cost beside an $800,000 plant. It requires digital skills a flat, laissez-faire partnership may lack, and bulk aggregate orders still need logistics and personal account management, so online sales alone cannot fill the 120,000-unit capacity.

Construction industry event sponsorship: A presence at a sector event gives face-to-face contact with engineers and specifiers and can showcase the new screening plant, supporting the 54% who check credentials. Stand and travel costs are high for a partnership servicing a $520,000 loan, and one event cannot sustain year-round orders given the $420,000 fixed-cost base.

Recommendation: QRAG should prioritise direct tendering to civil engineers, supported by a simple online information page. Tendering directly converts the survey's certified-standard demand into contracts and suits a relationship-based partnership. Event sponsorship is rejected as expensive and short-lived; a full online platform is rejected because aggregate buying remains relationship-driven and the 3.9% contamination rate means engineers need assurance before ordering online.

It also creates repeat-bid relationships that an event cannot sustain.

level_1_1_to_4: Limited awareness of the three marketing options with minimal QRAG context.
level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to QRAG's survey and costs.
level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why events and online-only are rejected.

questions.question_text: QRAG has high absenteeism and a 3.9% contamination defect rate. Explain two ways team working could help.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Organising the 42 site staff into teams for the new screening plant encourages shared responsibility for grading, so peers can spot contamination early and reduce the 3.9% defect rate and the 4.6% site waste. Team norms also discourage absenteeism, because colleagues rely on each other to keep the 120,000-unit output on schedule.

Point 2: Team working fits QRAG's flat structure and laissez-faire leadership, letting the 16 staff needing on-the-job training learn from experienced colleagues at no course cost beyond the $700 college option. Shared problem-solving raises commitment and helps the two partners hold delivery time at 3.8 days while the $520,000 loan is serviced from the $6.00 contribution.

Teams can also share the 16 untrained staff across shifts so learning happens during normal work, protecting the 3.8-day delivery time. This suits a partnership of 42 where the two owners cannot supervise every site directly, and it turns the $700 course into a shared resource rather than a one-off cost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid way team working helps (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to QRAG's absenteeism, defects and structure.

questions.question_text: A training review shows 16 of 42 QRAG site staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new screening plant. Consider promoting a trained operative internally or recruiting a screening supervisor externally. Which should QRAG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal promotion: Promoting an experienced operative who already knows the screening plant rewards loyalty and can reduce absenteeism among the 42 staff, while keeping the flat, laissez-faire culture. It is cheap and fast, and the promoted worker can coach the 16 still untrained. The risk is that the operative lacks supervisory skills, and promoting one person does not fill the wider skills gap or guarantee the 3.9% contamination rate falls.

External recruitment: A qualified supervisor could impose grading discipline immediately, cut the 3.9% defect rate and bring formal systems to a partnership with high absenteeism. Advertising, selection and induction cost money and time on top of a $520,000 loan, and an outsider may struggle with QRAG's informal laissez-faire style; with 16 of 42 untrained, new hires alone do not solve the problem.

Decision: QRAG should promote internally and add a short college course at $700 for the new supervisor. Internal promotion is low-cost, motivates the 42-strong workforce and uses existing knowledge of the screening plant, directly addressing absenteeism. External recruitment is rejected because its cost and cultural-fit risk are high and it leaves the 16 untrained operatives unsupported, so contamination defects would likely persist.

Internal promotion also signals to the 42 staff that skill and loyalty are rewarded, which matters where absenteeism is high. The $700 course can give the new supervisor formal grading knowledge without the cost of a full external salary. QRAG should review the 3.9% contamination rate after one quarter; if it has not improved, a short-term specialist could then be brought in on clear terms.

level_1_1_to_4: Basic comparison of internal promotion and external recruitment with limited QRAG application.
level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of cost, speed and cultural fit of both options using QRAG's training and defect data.
level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision referencing cost, absenteeism and contamination.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how QRAG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $10.00) = $420,000 ÷ $6.00 = 70,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 70,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $10.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways the management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare break-even of 70,000 units with output of 120,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 50,000 units, so the partners can judge how much demand may fall before losses while absenteeism is high.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution to assess tenders: the 61% of 450 engineers who would specify certified recycled aggregate may justify a small price concession, and managers can calculate how much volume is needed to keep total contribution above the $420,000 fixed costs.
3. Link the 70,000-unit break-even point to the $520,000 bank loan, setting a minimum output that covers fixed costs and interest before the $800,000 plant is worked at full capacity.
4. Track average total cost of $13.50 a unit ($420,000 ÷ 120,000 = $3.50 plus $10.00) against 4.6% site waste, 3.9% contamination and 9.4% input inflation, so the partners can target the $700 training where it protects margin most.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 70,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 50,000 units against 120,000 output; tender pricing on $6.00 contribution for the 61% certified segment; loan-service volume for the $520,000 loan; and average total cost benchmarking at $13.50 to monitor 4.6% waste and 9.4% inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QRAG's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed for 2024 and 2025. Has QRAG's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 38.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of 1,050 on revenue of 3,000 gives 35.0% in 2024, and 1,368 on 3,600 gives 38.0% in 2025. Operating profit of 450 on revenue of 3,000 gives 15.0%, and 576 on 3,600 gives 16.0%. Operating profit of 450 on capital employed of 2,500 gives 18.0%, and 576 on 3,200 gives 18.0%. Revenue rose by 600, cost of sales rose by 282, and interest payable rose from 50 to 64.

Evaluation: The trading margins improved but the return on the enlarged capital base did not. The 35.0% to 38.0% gross margin shows better control of direct costs despite 9.4% fuel and machinery inflation and 4.6% site waste. The 15.0% to 16.0% operating margin also rose, since operating profit increased by 126 while revenue rose by 600, so overheads were broadly controlled. However the 18.0% ROCE was unchanged: capital employed grew from 2,500 to 3,200 with the $800,000 crushing plant, and operating profit grew in the same proportion, so the extra investment has not yet raised efficiency. Interest payable rose from 50 to 64 with the $520,000 loan.

Conclusion: QRAG's financial performance has improved only in its trading margins, not overall, because ROCE is flat at 18.0%. The $800,000 plant has increased profit but not the return on capital, and higher interest payable adds pressure. The partners should raise utilisation of the 120,000-unit capacity and cut the 3.9% contamination rate so that operating profit grows faster than the new capital base before judging the investment a success.

level_1_1_to_4: States isolated figures from Appendix 2 without accurate calculation.
level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three measures for both years accurately and describes the trend with some QRAG context.
level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion that ROCE being flat limits the improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QRAG of supplying recycled aggregate.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled aggregate matches the 61% of 450 surveyed civil engineers who would specify more if it met a certified standard and the 54% who check environmental credentials, protecting the $16.00 price and $6.00 contribution while fuel and machinery costs rise 9.4%. It also aligns QRAG with the 3.6% growth in infrastructure spending and the $800,000 plant.

Disadvantage: Contamination of 3.9% and 4.6% site waste can raise the $10.00 variable cost through re-screening and re-handling, and with 16 of 42 staff untrained and $700 course costs, consistent certified quality is hard to guarantee. If engineers reject a batch, QRAG risks complaints and lost tenders just as the $520,000 loan repayments begin, squeezing returns on the new plant.

QRAG should therefore secure contracts that specify the certified standard before committing more of the $800,000 plant capacity, and monitor whether the 54% credential check translates into actual tenders won rather than stated preference alone, which would protect the $6.00 contribution.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using QRAG's survey, costs and defect data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in fuel and machinery input costs will affect QRAG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If the $520,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra cost is 0.75% of $520,000 = $3,900 a year (0.0075 x $520,000), which is small against $420,000 fixed costs; if the loan is fixed-rate, the immediate effect is zero. Appendix 2 shows interest payable rising from 50 to 64, so QRAG is already more exposed to debt, and higher rates could also slow the 3.6% infrastructure growth, but fixing the rate would cap this risk.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.77 an hour): The workforce of 42 means wage costs rise across site roles. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage bill can be invented. The defensible comparison is productivity: 120,000 units divided by 42 workers is about 2,857 tonnes per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or improves; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $6.00 contribution falls, worsening the high-absenteeism problem.

Fuel and machinery costs (9.4%): An illustrative upper bound is that the whole $10.00 variable cost rises 9.4%, adding $0.94 a unit (0.094 x $10.00 = $0.94), which at 120,000 units is about $112,800 a year (120,000 x $0.94). Even partial pass-through would significantly reduce the $6.00 contribution needed to service the $520,000 loan. The certified-standard demand from 61% of engineers may allow some price recovery, but it is unlikely to offset the full amount.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in fuel and machinery input costs has the greatest impact. It compounds across all 120,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution on which the $800,000 plant depends, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $3,900 and the wage effect can be managed through productivity. QRAG should prioritise energy efficiency and certified pricing to recover the increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited identification of the external factors with minimal application to QRAG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the impact of at least two of the three changes on QRAG's costs, revenue or financing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
